The first reads: "RULES OF CIVIL PROCEDURE FOR THE UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURTS 1 Effective September 16, 1938, as amended to December 1, 2024 TITLE I."

question: Y136
answer:
# DRAFT FOR ATTORNEY REVIEW — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

**Instrument and jurisdiction.** Council of Europe treaty regime: the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (ECHR), Rome, 4 November 1950, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15, governing the European Court of Human Rights (Strasbourg). This is public international law binding the High Contracting Parties; it is not the domestic law of any State, and nothing here is assumed to carry over to any other court or jurisdiction.

---

## 1. Question presented

In the Convention text presented as amended through Protocol No. 15, (a) for what term is a judge of the European Court of Human Rights elected, and (b) may a judge be re-elected? A training slide asserts that judges serve renewable six-year terms.

## 2. Short answer

**(a) Term: nine years. (b) Re-election: not permitted.** Article 23(1) of the consolidated text reads: *"The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected."*

The slide is wrong on **both** elements. The renewable six-year term it describes has not been the governing rule since 31 May 2010. Two independent errors should be corrected in the training material, not one.

---

## 3. Controlling text

### 3.1 Which text controls, and why the phrase "as amended through Protocol No. 15" must be read cumulatively

The Court publishes a single consolidated edition. Its front matter states:

> "The text of the Convention is presented as amended by the provisions of Protocol No. 15 (CETS No. 213) as from its entry into force on 1 August 2021 and of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194) as from its entry into force on 1 June 2010. The text of the Convention had previously been amended according to the provisions of Protocol No. 3 (ETS No. 45), which entered into force on 21 September 1970, of Protocol No. 5 (ETS No. 55), which entered into force on 20 December 1971, and of Protocol No. 8 (ETS No. 118), which entered into force on 1 January 1990 … All provisions which had been amended or added by these Protocols were replaced by Protocol No. 11 (ETS No. 155), as from the date of its entry into force on 1 November 1998."
> — Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15, and supplemented by Protocols Nos. 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 16 (Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights, official consolidated edition, text as amended from 1 August 2021), front matter — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG (accessed 23 November 2026).

*Point to record for the file:* "as amended through Protocol No. 15" means the cumulative consolidated text (Protocols 3, 5, 8, 11, 14, 15), not Protocol No. 15's amendments applied in isolation to an earlier text. A non-cumulative reading would yield an Article 23(1) reading "six years … may be re-elected" — a text no depositary maintains and which the Court's own edition contradicts. The cumulative reading is the only defensible one. Note that this interpretive point does **not** change the answer: Protocol No. 15 did not touch the length of the term or re-eligibility (see §4), so Article 23(1) reads "nine years … may not be re-elected" under either the Protocol-14 or the Protocol-15 state of the text.

### 3.2 Article 23 — the operative provision, quoted in full

> **"ARTICLE 23**
> **Terms of office and dismissal**
> 1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.
> 2. The judges shall hold office until replaced. They shall, however, continue to deal with such cases as they already have under consideration.
> 3. No judge may be dismissed from office unless the other judges decide by a majority of two-thirds that that judge has ceased to fulfil the required conditions."
> — ECHR, consolidated edition as amended from 1 August 2021, Art. 23 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG.

### 3.3 Article 21 — criteria for office (context; explains where the age rule went)

> **"ARTICLE 21**
> **Criteria for office**
> 1. The judges shall be of high moral character and must either possess the qualifications required for appointment to high judicial office or be jurisconsults of recognised competence.
> 2. Candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly, further to Article 22.
> 3. The judges shall sit on the Court in their individual capacity.
> 4. During their term of office the judges shall not engage in …" [text continues; truncated in the retrieved source]
> — ECHR, consolidated edition as amended from 1 August 2021, Art. 21 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG.

### 3.4 Article 22 — mode of election (context)

> "According to Article 22 of the Convention 'The judges shall be elected by the Parliamentary Assembly with respect to each High Contracting Party by a majority of votes cast from a list of three candidates nominated by the High Contracting Party'."
> — Procedure for the election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights, SG-AS (2026) 01, para. 13 — https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf.

### 3.5 Article 25 — a different "re-election" question, flagged so it is not conflated

> **"ARTICLE 25**
> **Plenary Court**
> The plenary Court shall
> (a) elect its President and one or two Vice-Presidents for a period of three years; they may be re-elected;
> …
> (c) elect the Presidents of the Chambers of the Court; they may be re-elected;"
> — ECHR, consolidated edition as amended from 1 August 2021, Art. 25 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG.

Article 25's express permission of re-election for the Court's internal offices is a deliberate contrast with Article 23(1)'s prohibition on re-election of judges *to the Court*. Training material should not present these as in tension.

---

## 4. What each amendment actually did

| Topic | Before 1 June 2010 (Protocol No. 11 text) | In the text as amended through Protocol No. 15 |
|---|---|---|
| Length of term | Six years | **Nine years** — Art. 23(1), 1st sentence |
| Re-election | Permitted | **Prohibited** — Art. 23(1), 2nd sentence |
| Age at end of term | Term expired on the judge reaching 70 (former Art. 23(2): *"The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70"*) | That paragraph **deleted** by Protocol No. 15, Art. 2(3); age control moved to the candidacy stage: candidates must be under 65 when the list of three is requested (new Art. 21(2)) |
| Holding over | Hold office until replaced; continue with cases in hand (former Art. 23(3)) | Same rule, now Art. 23(2) |
| Dismissal | Two-thirds majority of the judges (former Art. 23(4)) | Same rule, now Art. 23(3) |

*The "Before 1 June 2010" column is drawn from the amendment history and from footnote 26 of SG-AS (2026) 01; the pre-2010 wording of Article 23(1) itself must be verified against CETS No. 155 / CETS No. 194 before this table is published (see §7 and §9).*

Protocol No. 15's amending text, verbatim on the point:

> **"Article 2**
> 1 In Article 21 of the Convention, a new paragraph 2 shall be inserted, which shall read as follows:
> 'Candidates shall be less than 65 years of age at the date by which the list of three candidates has been requested by the Parliamentary Assembly, further to Article 22.'
> 2 Paragraphs 2 and 3 of Article 21 of the Convention shall become paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 21 respectively.
> **3 Paragraph 2 of Article 23 of the Convention shall be deleted. Paragraphs 3 and 4 of Article 23 shall become paragraphs 2 and 3 of Article 23 respectively.**"
> — Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 213, Strasbourg, 24 June 2013 (in force 1 August 2021), Art. 2 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_eng.

And the confirming footnote in the Parliamentary Assembly's own election procedure:

> "26 Former paragraph 2 of Article 23 ('The terms of office of judges shall expire when they reach the age of 70') was deleted by Protocol 15."
> — SG-AS (2026) 01, n.26 — https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf.

**Conclusion on amendment history: Protocol No. 15 did not change the term of office or the prohibition on re-election.** It removed the age-70 cut-off and re-cast the age rule as a candidacy condition. Anyone attributing the nine-year single term to Protocol No. 15 would be wrong as to provenance, even though the answer under the Protocol-15 text is the same.

---

## 5. Where the slide's rule came from, and when it stopped being the law

The six-year renewable term corresponds to the text in force **from 1 November 1998 (Protocol No. 11) until 31 May 2010**. The nine-year single non-renewable term took effect on **1 June 2010**, with the entry into force of Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194).

The Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15 confirms, from the Council of Europe's own side, that non-renewability was already the position by 2013:

> "This modification aims at enabling highly qualified judges to serve the full nine-year term of office and thereby reinforce the consistency of the membership of the Court. The age limit applied under Article 23, paragraph 2 of the Convention, as drafted prior to the entry into force of this Protocol, had the effect of preventing certain experienced judges from completing their term of office. It was considered no longer essential to impose an age limit, given the fact that judges' terms of office are no longer renewable."
> — Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15, para. 12 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng.

A slide describing renewable six-year terms is therefore roughly sixteen years out of date and should be withdrawn from circulation, not merely annotated.

---

## 6. Temporal points that must go into the training material

**(a) Protocol No. 15's transitional provision touches only the age rules, not the term.** Article 8(1) of Protocol No. 15 provides:

> "1 The amendments introduced by Article 2 of this Protocol shall apply only to candidates on lists submitted to the Parliamentary Assembly by the High Contracting Parties under Article 22 of the Convention after the entry into force of this Protocol."
> — Protocol No. 15, CETS No. 213, Art. 8(1) — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_eng.

Consequences, per the Explanatory Report:

> "Candidates appearing on previously submitted lists, by extension including judges in office and judges-elect at the date of entry into force of the Protocol, will continue to be subject to the rule applying before the entry into force of the present Protocol, namely the expiry of their term of office when they reach the age of 70."
> — Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15, para. 15 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng.

So a judge elected from a list submitted before 1 August 2021 may still be subject to the age-70 expiry rule. That is a statement about **when a term ends**, not about its length or renewability — the nine-year, non-renewable rule applies to all of them.

**(b) "Nine years" is the election term, not a guaranteed length of service.** Article 23(2) keeps a judge in office until replaced, and requires the judge to continue with cases already under consideration. Actual service can therefore exceed nine years. If the training deck uses the term to compute service or retirement dates, this must be stated.

**(c) Judges elected before 1 June 2010.** The Protocol No. 14 transitional arrangements for judges then in office were not in the retrieved source set. Do not tell trainees that every judge now sitting was elected for nine years; pull CETS No. 194 before any such statement is made.

**(d) Mid-term vacancies — open point.** The Convention text does not address whether a judge elected to fill a vacancy for the balance of a predecessor's term may subsequently be elected for a full nine-year term. Do not assert a position in training material without checking the Parliamentary Assembly's current practice under Resolution 2648 (2026) on the procedure for the election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights (cited as a relevant text in SG-AS (2026) 01; not itself in the retrieved source set).

---

## 7. Authority assessment — where it is solid and where it is thin

**Solid.** Article 23(1) is quoted verbatim from the Court's official consolidated edition, and the same words are reproduced by the Parliamentary Assembly's election-procedure document: "Article 23 of the Convention, as amended by Protocol No. 15 to the Convention, stipulates: '1. The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected.'" (SG-AS (2026) 01, para. 13). The provision is unambiguous on its face; there is no construction question.

**Thin — provenance only.** The proposition that the nine-year single term was introduced by Protocol No. 14 is an **inference**, not a quotation: the Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15 (para. 12) states that terms "are no longer renewable", and the only amending instrument between 1 June 2010 and Protocol No. 15 is Protocol No. 14 (CETS No. 194). The text of CETS No. 194, Article 2, was not in the retrieved source set. It must be pulled and checked before the provenance sentence in §5 or the "before" column in §4 is published externally. This does not affect the answer to either question, which rests on the consolidated Article 23(1).

**No conflicting authority located.** No judgment or advisory opinion construing Article 23(1) was found, and none is expected: the provision is self-executing and its wording admits of no alternative reading. The Court's Advisory Opinions of 12 February 2008 and 22 January 2010 concern lists of candidates under Article 22, not terms of office. If the team wants a judicial citation for the non-renewability rule, none should be manufactured.

**Language.** The English text is quoted. The French authentic text should be checked before any bilingual publication of the slide.

---

## 8. Corrected slide text (drop-in replacement)

> **Judges of the European Court of Human Rights**
> Judges are elected by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe from a list of three candidates nominated by each High Contracting Party (ECHR Art. 22).
> **Term: nine years, single and non-renewable.** "The judges shall be elected for a period of nine years. They may not be re-elected." (ECHR Art. 23(1), as amended; nine-year single term in force since 1 June 2010, carried unchanged into the text as amended by Protocol No. 15, in force 1 August 2021.)
> **Holding over:** a judge whose term ends remains in office until replaced and continues to deal with cases already under consideration (Art. 23(2)).
> **Superseded rule:** the earlier six-year renewable term was abolished with effect from 1 June 2010. Any material stating that judges serve renewable six-year terms is out of date.

---

## 9. Verification checklist before this draft goes out

1. Pull Protocol No. 14, CETS No. 194, Art. 2 and confirm the wording that replaced Article 23(1) — needed for §4 ("before" column) and §5 (provenance).
2. Pull Protocol No. 14's transitional provisions and confirm how judges in office on 1 June 2010 were treated.
3. Confirm the pre-2010 Article 23(1) wording against Protocol No. 11, CETS No. 155 (the six-year renewable rule and its first-election staggering).
4. Check the French authentic text of Article 23(1) if the slide is bilingual.
5. Confirm the current Parliamentary Assembly practice on mid-term vacancies (Resolution 2648 (2026)) before answering §6(d).
6. Re-verify the consolidated text against the Court's edition at the date of publication — the edition is updated as protocols enter into force.

---

## Sources cited in full

1. Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, Rome, 4 November 1950, as amended by Protocols Nos. 11, 14 and 15 and supplemented by Protocols Nos. 1, 4, 6, 7, 12, 13 and 16 (Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights, official consolidated edition, text as amended from 1 August 2021), front matter and Arts. 21, 22, 23, 25 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG (accessed 23 November 2026).
2. Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 213, Strasbourg, 24 June 2013 (in force 1 August 2021), Arts. 2, 7, 8 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_eng.
3. Explanatory Report to Protocol No. 15 amending the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, CETS No. 213, paras 10–15 — https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/protocol_15_explanatory_report_eng.
4. Procedure for the election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights, SG-AS (2026) 01 (Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe), paras 12–13 and n.26 — https://rm.coe.int/procedure-for-the-election-of-judges-to-the-european-court-of-human-ri/1680aa8ddf.
5. Protocol No. 14 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, amending the control system of the Convention, CETS No. 194, Strasbourg, 13 May 2004 (in force 1 June 2010) — text not in the retrieved source set; cited on the strength of source 1 (front matter) and source 3 (para. 12); Art. 2 and the transitional provisions to be pulled and checked.
6. Protocol No. 11 to the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, restructuring the control machinery established thereby, CETS No. 155, Strasbourg, 11 May 1994 (in force 1 November 1998) — cited per source 1 (front matter); Art. 23 text to be pulled if the deck requires the pre-2010 wording.
7. Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, Resolution 2648 (2026) on the procedure for the election of judges to the European Court of Human Rights — cited as a relevant text in source 4; not itself in the retrieved source set.

*This memorandum is a draft prepared for review by a qualified attorney. It is not legal advice and should not be relied on or circulated in its current form.*

question: Y137
answer:
PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — DRAFT FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY — NOT LEGAL ADVICE

MEMORANDUM

To: State-aid team
Re: (1) Whether Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 (the 'GBER') can be relied on to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from notification; (2) which instrument the GBER's scope passage identifies as governing that aid
Jurisdiction: European Union — State aid under Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union ('TFEU'). This note states no view on the law of any other jurisdiction.

====================================================================
I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
====================================================================

1. Can a State-aid team rely on the GBER to exempt aid to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive coal mine from the notification obligation in Article 108(3) TFEU?

2. If not, which instrument does the GBER's scope passage identify as dealing with that aid?

====================================================================
II. SHORT ANSWERS
====================================================================

1. **No.** Aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines is expressly and categorically excluded from the GBER's scope by Article 1(3)(d) of Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014, and by recital 12. The GBER confers no block exemption for it. Such aid must be notified to the Commission under Article 108(3) TFEU (subject only to Section IV.H below) and assessed individually.

2. **Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24** (CELEX 32010D0787). The GBER names it twice — in Article 1(3)(d) ('as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787') and in recital 12 ('which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines').

====================================================================
III. GOVERNING INSTRUMENTS — FULL CITATIONS
====================================================================

[A] Commission Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 of 17 June 2014 declaring certain categories of aid compatible with the internal market in application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty (Text with EEA relevance), OJ L 187, 26.6.2014, p. 1–78 ('GBER').

[B] Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24–29 (CELEX 32010D0787).

[C] Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, Articles 107, 108 and 109 (consolidated version, OJ C 202, 7.6.2016, p. 47).

[D] Council Regulation (EU) 2015/1588 of 13 July 2015 on the application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to certain categories of horizontal State aid (codification), OJ L 248, 24.7.2015, p. 1 — the enabling regulation under which the GBER was adopted.

[E] Council Regulation (EU) 2015/1589 of 13 July 2015 laying down detailed rules for the application of Article 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (codification), OJ L 248, 24.7.2015, p. 9 — in particular Article 16 (recovery of unlawful aid).

[F] Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/2831 of 13 December 2023 on the application of Articles 107 and 108 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union to de minimis aid, OJ L, 2023/2831, 15.12.2023 — mentioned only for completeness at Section IV.H.3.

====================================================================
IV. ANALYSIS
====================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------
A. The GBER is a block exemption: its scope is exhaustive and cannot be extended by analogy
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Article 108(4) TFEU empowers the Commission to adopt regulations declaring that certain categories of aid are exempt from the notification obligation in Article 108(3) TFEU. The GBER was adopted on that basis, within the framework of Council Regulation (EU) 2015/1588 [D].

The legal effect is binary. If a measure falls within the GBER's material, sectoral, temporal and threshold conditions, it is exempt from prior notification and is lawful without a Commission decision. If it falls outside — for any reason, including a sectoral exclusion in Article 1 — the exemption simply does not attach, and the default rule in Article 108(3) TFEU applies: the Member State 'shall not put its proposed measures into effect until this procedure has resulted in a final decision.'

A block exemption is not a set of guidelines capable of purposive extension. There is no scope for a State-aid team to argue that coal-closure aid is 'in the spirit of' the GBER, or that the GBER's environmental-protection or regional-aid chapters can be read across. The Commission has no power to exempt outside the categories fixed in the enabling regulation and the GBER's own Article 1. Reliance on an inapplicable block exemption does not produce an exempt measure; it produces unnotified aid.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
B. The GBER's scope passage excludes coal-closure aid in express terms
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Article 1 of the GBER fixes scope. Article 1(1) lists the categories of aid to which the Regulation applies ((a) regional aid through (l) aid for local infrastructures). Article 1(2) begins 'This Regulation shall not apply to:' with point (a) addressing aid schemes whose average annual State aid budget exceeds EUR 150 million. Article 1(3) then sets out the sectoral exclusions, and its point (d) reads, verbatim:

  '(d) aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787;'

Point (e) of the same paragraph excludes 'the categories of regional aid excluded in Article 13'.

The closing subparagraph of Article 1(3) provides:

  'Where an undertaking is active in the excluded sectors as referred to in points (a), (b) or (c) of the first subparagraph and in sectors which fall within the scope of this Regulation, this Regulation applies to aid granted in respect of the latter sectors or activities, provided that Member States ensure by appropriate means, such as separation of activities or distinction of costs, that the activities in the excluded sectors do not benefit from the aid granted in accordance with this Regulation.'

Two points follow from the wording of that subparagraph. First, it is addressed only to points (a), (b) and (c) (fisheries and aquaculture; primary agricultural production; processing and marketing of agricultural products). Coal appears at point (d) and is deliberately not included in the separation-of-activities carve-out. Second, the consequence is that a coal producer cannot 'ring-fence' its way into the GBER for closure aid: there is no mechanism in Article 1(3) by which coal-closure aid can be brought within scope by separating accounts. Article 1(3)(d) is a clean exclusion.

Recital 12 of the GBER confirms the intent in unambiguous language:

  '(12) This Regulation should not apply to aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, which is dealt with by the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines. This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.'

The GBER's own definitional Article reinforces the linkage: Article 2(13) defines 'coal' by reference to 'the international codification system for coal established by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe and clarified in the Council decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'.

**Conclusion on Question 1: the answer is No, and it is No on the face of the Regulation.** The exclusion is not a matter of interpretation, of proportionality, or of the Commission's discretion. It is an express sectoral carve-out.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
C. The instrument identified by the scope passage
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The GBER's scope passage does not merely exclude coal-closure aid; it names the instrument that deals with it. Article 1(3)(d) refers to 'Council Decision No 2010/787'. Recital 12 spells the reference out in full: 'the Council Decision of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'.

The instrument is:

  **Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24.**

(Publications Office identifiers: CELEX 32010D0787; ELI dec/2010/787/oj; OJ identifier JOL_2010_336_R_0024_01.)

That Decision was adopted by the Council, on a proposal from the Commission, on the basis of Article 107(3)(e) TFEU — the provision under which the Council may, by decision, determine categories of aid that are compatible with the internal market. (Legal basis to be confirmed against the Decision's preamble: see the verification checklist, Section V.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
D. What Decision 2010/787/EU actually provides
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The Decision is the lex specialis for coal. Its operative provisions, as relevant here:

**Article 1 — definitions.**
  '(a) "coal" means high-grade, medium-grade and low-grade category A and B coal within the meaning of the international codification system for coal laid down by the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe;
   (b) "closure" means the permanent cessation of production and sale of coal;
   (c) "closure plan" means a plan drawn up by a Member State providing for measures culminating in the definitive closure of coal production units;
   (d) "coal production unit" means underground or opencast coal workings and related infrastructure capable of producing raw coal independently of other parts of the undertaking;
   (e) "coal year" means calendar year or another 12-month period used as a reference for contracts in the coal industry;
   ...
   (g) "current production losses" means the positive difference between the coal production cost and the selling price at utilisation point freely agreed between the contracting parties in the light of the conditions prevailing on the world market.'

**Article 2 — principle.**
  '(1) In the context of closure of uncompetitive mines, aid to the coal industry may be considered compatible with the proper functioning of the internal market if it complies with the provisions of this Decision.
   (2) Aid shall cover only costs in connection with coal for the production of electricity, the combined production of heat and electricity, the production of coke and the fuelling of blast furnaces in the steel industry, where such use takes place in the Union.'

**Article 3 — closure aid (current production losses).**
  '(1) Aid to an undertaking intended specifically to cover the current production losses of coal production units may be considered compatible with the internal market only if it satisfies the following conditions:
   (a) the operation of the coal production units concerned must form part of a closure plan the deadline of which does not extend beyond 31 December 2018;
   ...'

**Article 3(3) — recovery on non-compliance with the closure plan.**
  'If the coal production units to which aid is granted pursuant to paragraph 1 are not closed at the date fixed in the closure plan as authorised by the Commission, the Member State concerned shall recover all aid granted in respect of the whole period covered by the closure plan.'

**Article 4 — aid to cover exceptional costs.**
  '(1) State aid granted to undertakings which carry out or have carried out an activity in connection with coal production to enable them to cover the costs arising from or having arisen from the closure of coal production units and which are not related to current production, may be considered compatible with the internal market provided that the amount paid does not exceed such costs. Such aid may be used to cover:
   (a) the costs incurred and cost provisions made only by undertakings which are closing or have closed coal production units, including undertakings benefiting from closure aid;
   (b) the costs incurred by several undertakings.
   (2) The categories of costs covered by paragraph 1 are defined in the Annex. Paragraph 1 shall not apply to costs resulting from non-compliance with environmental regulations.'

Three features matter for the team's purposes. First, compatibility under the Decision is **conditional**, not automatic: it depends on a closure plan, a deadline, cost ceilings and the other conditions in Article 3(1). Second, the Decision is a **compatibility** instrument, not an exemption from notification — aid under it was notified to and authorised by the Commission (note the reference in Article 3(3) to 'the closure plan as authorised by the Commission'). Third, it is **time-limited**: Article 3(1)(a) fixes 31 December 2018 as the outer limit for the closure-plan deadline.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
E. Temporal application — the answer depends on the date the aid is granted
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The team's question cannot be answered at the level of principle alone; the applicable regime is date-sensitive. Three windows:

**E.1 Aid granted before 1 July 2014.**
The GBER entered into force on 1 July 2014 (Article 34 GBER: entry into force on the twentieth day following publication in the Official Journal; publication was 26 June 2014). Aid granted before that date could not have been exempted by the GBER at all. It fell to be assessed under Decision 2010/787/EU and the preceding regime (Regulation (EC) No 1407/2002 on State aid to the coal industry, which expired on 31 December 2010).

**E.2 Aid granted between 1 July 2014 and 31 December 2018.**
This is the window in which the GBER and Decision 2010/787/EU coexisted. During it, the answer to Question 1 was still No: Article 1(3)(d) and recital 12 excluded coal-closure aid from the GBER for the whole of that period. The route was notification under Article 108(3) TFEU and individual assessment against Decision 2010/787/EU, including the Article 3(1)(a) deadline of 31 December 2018.

**E.3 Aid granted after 31 December 2018.**
Decision 2010/787/EU was time-limited and ceased to apply at the end of 2018 (Article 3(1)(a) bars any closure plan extending beyond 31 December 2018; the Decision's final provisions likewise confine its application to that period — confirm the article number, see Section V). The GBER's exclusion of coal-closure aid is not, however, disapplied by the lapse of the Decision. The exclusion in Article 1(3)(d) operates by subject matter ('aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines'), and recital 12's second sentence — 'This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid' — confirms that the Regulation's drafters drew the line at closure aid, not at the coal sector generally. Coal-closure aid therefore remains outside the GBER after 2018.

The consequence is that for aid granted after 31 December 2018 there is **no sector-specific instrument named by the GBER and in force**. Such aid must be notified under Article 108(3) TFEU and assessed directly against Article 107 TFEU — most plausibly Article 107(3)(c) or (e) — on its own facts. Whether the Commission would look favourably on such aid, and on what conditions, is a separate question on which this note expresses no view (see Section V, item 3).

**E.4 Practical consequence.** The team should fix the date of grant before doing anything else. If the measure has already been put into effect in reliance on the GBER, and the date of grant falls in any of the three windows above, the aid was not exempt. See Section IV.G.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
F. What the GBER *does* still cover in the coal sector
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The exclusion is targeted, not blanket. Recital 12, second sentence: 'This Regulation should apply to other types of aid in the coal sector, with the exception of regional aid.' Article 1(3)(e) read with Article 13 confirms that regional aid to the coal sector is outside the GBER.

So a coal undertaking may in principle obtain GBER-covered aid for, for example, training, employment of disadvantaged workers, environmental protection investment, or research and development — provided the relevant chapter's own conditions are met. What it cannot obtain under the GBER is aid whose object is to facilitate the closure of an uncompetitive mine, i.e. aid covering current production losses under a closure plan, or aid covering the exceptional costs of closure. Those are the matters reserved to Decision 2010/787/EU (to 2018) and, thereafter, to individual notification.

This distinction matters in drafting: a measure labelled 'environmental aid' or 'training aid' that in substance funds the current production losses of a mine scheduled for closure will be characterised by its substance, not its label, and will fall within Article 1(3)(d).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
G. Consequences if the team relies on the GBER
--------------------------------------------------------------------

**G.1 No exemption.** The measure is not exempt. It is unnotified aid put into effect in breach of the standstill obligation in the last sentence of Article 108(3) TFEU.

**G.2 Recovery.** Under Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589 [E], the Commission may require the Member State to recover unlawful aid, with interest, from the beneficiary. Article 3(3) of Decision 2010/787/EU shows the same recovery logic operating within the sectoral regime itself where a closure plan is not honoured.

**G.3 Private enforcement.** The standstill obligation has direct effect. Competitors may sue in the national courts for recovery and damages; the national court is obliged to draw the consequences of the breach. (See, among many, Case C-354/90 Fédération Nationale du Commerce Extérieur des Produits Alimentaires and Syndicat National des Négociants et Transformateurs de Saumon v French Republic [1991] ECR I-5505, and Case C-39/94 SFEI and Others v La Poste [1996] ECR I-3547 — citations to be verified against the reporter before use.)

**G.4 No cure by the GBER's own machinery.** The GBER contains no ratification or retroactive-validation mechanism. Nor can the Commission 'apply the GBER by analogy' in an individual decision; it would have to assess compatibility under Article 107 TFEU directly.

**G.5 The exemption/compatibility distinction.** Exemption from notification and compatibility with Article 107(1) TFEU are different questions. The GBER answers both for in-scope aid. For coal-closure aid, the GBER answers neither; compatibility must be established, and it can only be established by the Commission.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
H. What the team should do instead
--------------------------------------------------------------------

**H.1 Check for an existing authorisation.** Before notifying afresh, check whether the Commission has already authorised, by decision, the Member State's coal-closure aid scheme under Decision 2010/787/EU. If individual aid is granted strictly within the terms of such an authorised scheme and before its expiry, no fresh notification may be required. This is the most commonly overlooked route and should be checked first. Any such authorisation will be time-limited, so confirm its expiry date against the date of grant.

**H.2 Notify under Article 108(3) TFEU.** Otherwise, notify. The notification is made on the Commission's standard State aid notification forms (Commission Regulation (EC) No 794/2004, Annex I — confirm the current version). For a measure granted after 31 December 2018, the notification must make the case under Article 107(3) TFEU directly, since no sectoral instrument remains.

**H.3 De minimis — theoretically available, practically not.** Regulation (EU) 2023/2831 [F] sets a ceiling of EUR 300,000 per undertaking over any three-year period (Article 3(2)). Coal is not among that Regulation's excluded sectors. In practice a coal-mine closure measure will exceed EUR 300,000 by orders of magnitude, and splitting a closure package into de minimis tranches to avoid notification would be an abuse. Note also that de minimis aid cannot be cumulated with aid for the same eligible costs.

**H.4 Do not re-label.** As noted at Section IV.F, re-labelling closure aid as environmental, training or regional aid does not change its character for Article 1(3)(d) purposes, and regional aid to coal is separately excluded.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
I. Version control — which text of the GBER governs
--------------------------------------------------------------------

The GBER has been amended repeatedly since 2014, including by Commission Regulation (EU) 2017/1088 of 14 June 2017, Commission Regulation (EU) 2020/972 of 2 July 2020, Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/1237 of 23 July 2021, and Commission Regulation (EU) 2023/1315 of 23 June 2023 (OJ references to be verified — see Section V).

The correct text to cite is the consolidated version in force **on the date the aid is granted**, not the original 2014 text and not the latest consolidation. The paragraph numbering within Article 1 has shifted between versions as points have been added to Article 1(2); a reader consulting a consolidated text should locate the exclusion by its wording rather than by paragraph number, and should cite recital 12 alongside it, since the recital text is stable.

The substantive point, however, does not turn on the amendment history: the exclusion of aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines from the GBER's scope has been a structural feature of the Regulation since adoption, and nothing in the amendments identified above purports to bring coal-closure aid within the block exemption. But the precise current wording of point (d) — in particular whether the words 'as covered by Council Decision No 2010/787' remain — could not be verified from the sources retrieved for this note and must be checked before the memorandum is finalised (Section V, item 1).

====================================================================
V. WHERE THE AUTHORITY IS THIN, UNVERIFIED, OR LIKELY TO BE CONTESTED
====================================================================

This section is deliberately blunt. The core answers to Questions 1 and 2 rest on verbatim text of the GBER and are not in doubt. The following points are either unverified or genuinely open and must be resolved before the note is relied on.

1. **Current wording of Article 1(3)(d) in the consolidated GBER.** The text quoted at Section IV.B is from the Regulation as originally adopted (2014). I could not verify from the retrieved sources whether the 2023 consolidation (Regulation (EU) 2023/1315) retains the cross-reference to Decision 2010/787 at point (d), or whether the reference was adjusted following the Decision's expiry. **Action:** pull the consolidated text on EUR-Lex for the version in force at the date of grant and quote it verbatim in the final note. The answer to Question 1 does not change either way; the answer to Question 2 is stated in the alternative — the GBER originally identified Decision 2010/787/EU, and that is the instrument the scope passage names.

2. **Article number of the temporal limitation in Decision 2010/787/EU.** Article 3(1)(a) (closure plan deadline not beyond 31 December 2018) is quoted verbatim from the retrieved text and is certain. The Decision's own final provision fixing its period of application was not in the retrieved extract, and I have deliberately not assigned it an article number. **Action:** confirm the article number and quote it.

3. **Whether any successor instrument exists after 31 December 2018.** I have found no successor to Decision 2010/787/EU, and the GBER names none. This is a negative finding and should not be stated as settled. **Action:** check the Commission's State aid register and the Official Journal for 2019–date for any Council decision, Commission communication or guidelines on coal-closure aid, and check whether the Commission has taken position on the post-2018 legal basis. If a successor exists, Section IV.E.3 must be revised.

4. **Legal basis of Decision 2010/787/EU.** Stated at Section IV.C as Article 107(3)(e) TFEU on the basis of the instrument's character as a Council compatibility decision. Not verified against the preamble in the retrieved text. **Action:** confirm.

5. **OJ page references for the amending regulations listed at Section IV.I.** The regulation numbers and dates are reliable; the OJ citations should be checked on EUR-Lex before use.

6. **Notification form reference.** Regulation (EC) No 794/2004, Annex I, is cited at Section IV.H.2 as the standard notification form. Confirm the current consolidated version and annex numbering.

7. **Case-law citations at Section IV.G.3.** The propositions are uncontroversial and long settled, but the reporter references should be checked before the note leaves the office.

8. **Interaction with Article 1(4).** Article 1(4) of the GBER excludes, among other things, aid schemes that do not explicitly exclude payment of individual aid to an undertaking subject to an outstanding recovery order. That is a separate and additional bar and is not analysed here; it is flagged because a coal-closure scheme that has previously been the subject of a recovery decision would engage it.

====================================================================
VI. SUMMARY OF ADVICE
====================================================================

1. The GBER cannot be relied on. Article 1(3)(d) of Regulation (EU) No 651/2014 excludes 'aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines' from the Regulation's scope, and recital 12 says so in terms. There is no interpretive route around an express sectoral exclusion in a block exemption regulation.

2. The instrument the scope passage identifies is **Council Decision 2010/787/EU of 10 December 2010 on State aid to facilitate the closure of uncompetitive coal mines, OJ L 336, 21.12.2010, p. 24**. That Decision supplies the compatibility conditions (Articles 2, 3 and 4) and the 31 December 2018 outer limit (Article 3(1)(a)).

3. The team's next step is to fix the date of grant. If it falls on or before 31 December 2018 and the aid was granted under a Commission-authorised scheme, check the scope and expiry of that authorisation. Otherwise, notify under Article 108(3) TFEU. If the date of grant is after 31 December 2018, there is no sectoral instrument and the notification must be built directly on Article 107 TFEU.

4. If the measure has already been implemented in reliance on the GBER, treat it as unnotified aid and take advice immediately on the exposure under Article 108(3) TFEU, Article 16 of Regulation (EU) 2015/1589, and the private-enforcement risk described at Section IV.G.3.

# RESEARCH MEMORANDUM — DRAFT FOR REVIEW BY A QUALIFIED ATTORNEY

**This is a research draft, not legal advice.** It is prepared for review and adaptation by a qualified attorney admitted in the relevant jurisdiction before any reliance or filing.

---

## I. Jurisdiction and governing instrument

**Jurisdiction:** Council of Europe — the Contracting States (High Contracting Parties) to the European Convention on Human Rights. The Convention is a multilateral treaty; it is not the municipal law of any single state, and the answer below is an answer in treaty interpretation within the ECHR system. Domestic legal effect is given by each Contracting State's own implementing instrument (e.g., in the United Kingdom, the Human Rights Act 1998, s. 1 and Sch. 1). Where a *specific* national emergency proclamation, derogation notice or detention regime is in issue, that instrument must be reviewed separately; the analysis below is the general doctrinal position.

**Governing instrument cited:** Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, opened for signature 4 November 1950, Rome, ETS No. 005, 213 UNTS 221 (entered into force 3 September 1953), as amended by Protocols No. 11 (ETS No. 155), No. 14 (ETS No. 194) and No. 15 (CETS No. 213) (the "ECHR" or the "Convention"). The Convention was concluded in English and in French, **both texts equally authentic** (final clause, Rome, 4 November 1950); the English text published by the Council of Europe / European Court of Human Rights is used here.

---

## II. The two questions and the short answers

### Question 1 — May a Contracting State, invoking Article 15 during a war, derogate from Article 3?

**No. It may not.** Article 15(2) ECHR places Article 3 in an express, closed list of provisions from which no derogation may be made under Article 15.

### Question 2 — What narrow Article 2 exception does the same non-derogation clause state?

**The exception is: "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war".** Article 15(2) ECHR permits no derogation from Article 2 **except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war**.

---

## III. The text

### A. Article 15 ECHR (Derogation in time of emergency) — full text

> "**ARTICLE 15**
> **Derogation in time of emergency**
>
> 1. In time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation any High Contracting Party may take measures derogating from its obligations under this Convention to the extent strictly required by the exigencies of the situation, provided that such measures are not inconsistent with its other obligations under international law.
>
> 2. No derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision.
>
> 3. Any High Contracting Party availing itself of this right of derogation shall keep the Secretary General of the Council of Europe fully informed of the measures which it has taken and the reasons therefor. It shall also inform the Secretary General of the Council of Europe when such measures have ceased to operate and the provisions of the Convention are again being fully executed."

Source: ECHR, Article 15, ETS No. 005, as published by the European Court of Human Rights (official English text), https://www.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr/Convention_ENG (fetched 23 November 2026; sha256 f4608f7ed2d5).

### B. Article 3 ECHR — full text

> "**ARTICLE 3**
> **Prohibition of torture**
> No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment."

Source: ECHR, Article 3, ETS No. 005.

### C. Article 2 ECHR — full text of the relevant paragraphs

> "**ARTICLE 2**
> **Right to life**
>
> 1. Everyone's right to life shall be protected by law. No one shall be deprived of his life intentionally save in the execution of a sentence of a court following his conviction of a crime for which this penalty is provided by law.
>
> 2. Deprivation of life shall not be regarded as inflicted in contravention of this Article when it results from the use of force which is no more than absolutely necessary:
> (a) in defence of any person from unlawful violence;
> (b) in order to effect a lawful arrest or to prevent the escape of a person lawfully detained;
> (c) in action lawfully taken for the purpose of quelling a riot or insurrection."

Source: ECHR, Article 2, ETS No. 005. (The second sentence of Article 2(1) is now of historical application only, having been superseded as to the death penalty by Protocol No. 6 (ETS No. 114) and Protocol No. 13 (CETS No. 187).)

---

## IV. Analysis

### A. Article 3 is absolutely non-derogable under Article 15

1. **Textual bar.** Article 15(2) ECHR states in terms that "[n]o derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from **Articles 3**, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision." The words "under this provision" confine the bar to derogation by way of Article 15; but Article 15 is the only derogation mechanism the Convention provides, so the practical effect is that Article 3 continues in full force during any war or public emergency. Source: ECHR, Article 15(2), ETS No. 005.

2. **The Court's own restatement.** The European Court of Human Rights' *Guide on Article 15 of the Convention – Derogation in time of emergency* (European Court of Human Rights, last update 31 August 2026), para. 38, restates the protected list as: "Article 2 (the right to life), except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war; Article 3 (the prohibition of torture and other forms of ill-treatment); Article 4 § 1 (the prohibition of slavery or servitude); and Article 7 (no punishment without law)"; and para. 40 states that the effect of Article 15 § 2 is "that the rights to which they refer continue to apply during any time of war or public emergency". (This Guide is the Court's own secondary restatement, not a primary source; it is cited as corroboration of the treaty text, which is itself primary.) Source: https://ks.echr.coe.int/documents/d/echr-ks/guide_art_15_eng (fetched 23 November 2026; sha256 41b3ee2b98cd).

3. **Article 3 admits of no exception, qualification or balancing in any circumstances.** The prohibition is drafted without any limitation clause, unlike Articles 8–11. The Court has repeatedly held that Article 3 enshrines one of the fundamental values of a democratic society and prohibits torture and inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment in absolute terms, including in the most difficult circumstances such as the fight against terrorism and organised crime: *Ireland v. the United Kingdom*, 18 January 1978, Series A no. 25; *Selmouni v. France* [GC], no. 25803/94, ECHR 1999-V; *Gäfgen v. Germany* [GC], no. 22978/05, ECHR 2010.

4. **A reservation cannot achieve what Article 15(2) forbids.** Reservations are governed by Article 57 ECHR, which permits only reservations in respect of particular provisions and forbids reservations of a general character; the Court has held that reservations must be construed strictly and that impermissible reservations are severable and without effect: ECHR, Article 57, ETS No. 005; *Beliös v. Switzerland*, 29 April 1988, Series A no. 132; *Loizidou v. Turkey* (Preliminary Objections), 23 March 1995, Series A no. 310. A reservation to Article 3 would in any event be incompatible with the object and purpose of the Convention.

5. **Reinforcement from the peremptory character of the prohibition.** The prohibition of torture has been characterised as a peremptory norm of international law (jus cogens): *Al-Adsani v. the United Kingdom* [GC], no. 35763/99, ECHR 2001-XI; *Prosecutor v. Furundžija*, ICTY, Case No. IT-95-17/1-T, Trial Chamber Judgment of 10 December 1998. This matters concretely because Article 15(1) ECHR itself conditions any derogation on the measures being "not inconsistent with [the State's] other obligations under international law".

6. **Consistency with the parallel UN regime.** Article 4(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (16 December 1966, 999 UNTS 171) makes Article 7 ICCPR (torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment) non-derogable; and Article 2(2) of the Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment (10 December 1984, 1465 UNTS 85) provides that "[n]o exceptional circumstances whatsoever, whether a state of war or a threat of war, internal political instability or any other public emergency, may be invoked as a justification of torture." See also Human Rights Committee, General Comment No. 29 on Article 4 (States of Emergency), CCPR/C/21/Rev.1/Add.11, 31 August 2001. A derogation purporting to reach Article 3 ECHR would therefore also breach the State's "other obligations under international law" for the purposes of Article 15(1) ECHR.

### B. The narrow Article 2 exception: "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war"

1. **The exception is textual and singular.** Article 15(2) ECHR carves out of the Article 2 non-derogation rule one category only: "**deaths resulting from lawful acts of war**". In other words, Article 2 is non-derogable **save** that, in wartime, a Contracting State may derogate to the extent that a death results from an act of war that is lawful. Source: ECHR, Article 15(2), ETS No. 005.

2. **What the exception does not do.** It does not authorise derogation in respect of deaths that are *not* lawful acts of war. A killing that violates the law of armed conflict — for example, the deliberate targeting of civilians, an attack that is indiscriminate, or the killing of detained persons — is not a "lawful act of war" and therefore remains within the unqualified protection of Article 2. This reading is compelled both by the word "lawful" in Article 15(2) and by the proviso in Article 15(1) that derogating measures must not be "inconsistent with [the State's] other obligations under international law" — which in an armed conflict includes the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 (75 UNTS 31 et seq.) and Additional Protocol I of 8 June 1977 (1125 UNTS 3).

3. **"Lawful" is measured by international humanitarian law.** The Convention does not define "lawful acts of war"; the only body of law that can supply the content of lawfulness in an armed conflict is IHL. The Court has accepted that it will interpret and apply Convention rights by reference to IHL where the facts arise in an armed conflict: *Hassan v. the United Kingdom* [GC], no. 29750/09, ECHR 2014; *Georgia v. Russia (II)* [GC], no. 38263/08, 21 January 2021.

4. **Do not confuse this with Article 2(2).** Article 2(2) ECHR (defence of persons from unlawful violence; effecting a lawful arrest or preventing escape; quelling a riot or insurrection) is a *general limitation* on Article 2 that operates at all times and is not a derogation. The exception stated in the *non-derogation clause* — the question asked — is exclusively "deaths resulting from lawful acts of war" in Article 15(2). A memorandum that answers Question 2 with the Article 2(2) list would be answering a different question.

5. **The same clause protects other provisions.** For completeness, Article 15(2) also makes non-derogable Article 4(1) (prohibition of slavery and servitude) and Article 7 (no punishment without law). Separate non-derogation clauses appear in Protocol No. 6 (ETS No. 114), Article 3 ("No derogation from the provisions of this Protocol shall be made under Article 15 of the Convention"); Protocol No. 7 (ETS No. 117), Article 4(3) (as to ne bis in idem); and Protocol No. 13 (CETS No. 187), Article 3.

### C. Conditions that apply even to a permissible derogation (brief)

A State invoking Article 15 must still satisfy Article 15(1) and (3): (i) the existence of a "time of war or other public emergency threatening the life of the nation" — a factual threshold for the State's margin of appreciation, but not one that is automatically met by the label "war": *Lawless v. Ireland (No. 3)*, 1 July 1961, Series A no. 3; *Ireland v. the United Kingdom*, 18 January 1978, Series A no. 25; *Brannigan and McBride v. the United Kingdom*, 26 May 1993, Series A no. 258-B; *Aksoy v. Turkey*, 18 December 1996, Reports of Judgments and Decisions 1996-VI; (ii) measures "strictly required by the exigencies of the situation" (the proportionality/ temporariness test in *Aksoy* and *Brannigan and McBride*); (iii) consistency with other international obligations; and (iv) notification to, and continuing information of, the Secretary General of the Council of Europe under Article 15(3). These conditions operate on the *permissible* derogations only; they cannot enlarge the list in Article 15(2).

---

## V. Where the authority is thin or conflicting — flagged plainly

1. **No ECtHR judgment construes "lawful acts of war" in Article 15(2).** The phrase has not, so far as the Court's published case law and its own Article 15 Guide disclose, been the subject of a reasoned judgment. The Court's Guide lists the exception (para. 38) without construing it. The interpretation in section IV.B above is therefore textual and systemic (Article 15(1)'s "other obligations under international law" proviso plus IHL), not the product of direct authority. **Counsel should verify the position on the date of use and treat this point as the weakest link in the chain.**

2. **Extraterritorial application of Article 15 is contested.** Whether a derogation can reach conduct outside the State's Article 1 jurisdiction, and how Article 15 interacts with the extraterritoriality case law (*Banković and Others v. Belgium and Others* [GC], no. 52207/99, ECHR 2001-XII; *Georgia v. Russia (II)* [GC], no. 38263/08, 21 January 2021), is unsettled. If the facts involve operations abroad, this must be analysed separately.

3. **A minority academic view** treats the "lawful acts of war" exception as functionally obsolete, on the basis that the Court now reads Article 2 through IHL and so a death that is a lawful act of war is already not a violation of Article 2. That view does not affect the answer to either question, but it affects how much work the exception is doing in a given case.

4. **Authentic texts.** The French text of Article 15(2) ("actes licites de guerre") should be checked alongside the English in any contested case; both texts are equally authentic.

## VI. Answer in filing-ready form

> **Q1.** No. Article 15(2) of the Convention (ETS No. 005) provides that "[n]o derogation from Article 2, except in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war, or from Articles 3, 4 (paragraph 1) and 7 shall be made under this provision." Article 3 is expressly named; a Contracting State therefore cannot derogate from the prohibition of torture and inhuman or degrading treatment under Article 15, in wartime or otherwise.
>
> **Q2.** The single narrow exception to the non-derogability of Article 2 stated in that same clause is "in respect of deaths resulting from lawful acts of war" — that is, deaths resulting from acts of war that are lawful under international humanitarian law. The exception does not reach unlawful killings, and it is distinct from the general limitation in Article 2(2).

1. ANSWER
Retrieve: UNCITRAL Model Law on Internarional Commercial Arbitration, adopted 21 June 1985, with the amendments adopted 7 July 2006 (commonly cited as the '1985 Model Law, as amended in 2006'). Standard citation: UNCITRAL Model Law on Internarional Commercial Arbitration (1985), with amendments as adopted in 2006, UN Doc. A/40/17, Annex I (1985), endorsed by GA Res. 40/72 (11 Dec. 1985), amended by UNCITRAL at its 39th session (7 July 2006) and commended by GA Res. 61/33 (4 Dec. 2006), UN Doc. A/RES/61/33.
Official text: https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration ; PDF: https://uncitral.un.org/sites/default/files/media-documents/uncitral/en/07-86998_ebook.pdf
Why this text and not another: UNCITRAL's own description of the instrument tracks the four topics in the request word for word. The official page states that the Model Law 'covers all stages of the arbitral process from the arbitration agreement, the composition and jurisdiction of the arbitral tribunal and the extent of court intervention through to the recognition and enforcement of the arbitral award' (https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/modellaw/commercial_arbitration, fetched 2026-11-23). That is the coverage map required by ask 1.

2. COVERAGE MAP — WHERE EACH OF THE FOUR TOPICS SITS IN THE 2006 TEXT
(Article numbers are to the 1985 Model Law as amended in 2006. The 2006 revision touched only arts. 1(2), 7 and 35(2), inserted a new Chapter IV A replacing art. 17, and inserted a new art. 2 A — per the same official page; do not attribute any other provision to the 2006 revision.)
(a) Arbitration agreement — Chapter II. Art. 7 (definition and form; the 2006 revision modernised the writing requirement and is issued in two alternatives, Option I and Option II — see §5 below); art. 8 (court before which an action is brought on a matter covered by the agreement shall, on a party's request not later than its first statement on the substance, refer the parties to arbitration unless it finds the agreement null and void, inoperative or incapable of being performed); art. 9 (a court may order interrim measures of protection before or during arbitration — this is a court-power provision, not a tribunal-power provision).
(b) Composition and jurisdiction of the tribunal — Chapters III and IV. Arts. 10-15 (number of arbitrators; appointment, including court appointment under art. 11(3)-(4) and the mechanism for three-arbitrator appointments; grounds for challenge; challenge procedure, with court decision under art. 13(3); termination of mandate for failure or impossibility to act, with court decision under art. 14; appointment of a substitute arbitrator). Art. 16 (competence-competence: the tribunal may rule on its own jurisdiction, including objections to the existence or validity of the arbitration clause; the arbitration clause is treated as independent of the contract; a plea to jurisdiction must be raised not later than the statement of defence; a preliminary ruling on jurisdiction is subject to recourse to the court designated under art. 6, whose decision is not subject to appeal). Interim measures by the tribunal sit in Chapter IV A (arts. 17, 17 A-17 J), inserted in 2006.
(c) Court intervention — art. 5 (in matters governed by the Model Law no court shall intervene except where the Model Law so provides) read with art. 6 (each enacting State designates the court or other authority competent to perform the assistance and supervision functions). The permitted heads of intervention are then distributed across arts. 8, 9, 11(3)-(4), 13(3), 14, 16(3), 17 H-17 I (court-ordered interrim measures in the 2006 text), 27 (court assistance in taking evidence) and 34 (setting aside).
(d) Recognition and enforcement of the award — Chapter VIII. Art. 35 (an arbitral award, irrespective of the country in which it was made, shall be recognised as binding and, on application to the competent court, enforced, subject to arts. 35 and 36; the 2006 revision of art. 35(2) relaxed the documentary conditions — the party relying on the award supplies the original award or a copy and the original arbitration agreement or a copy, with a translation where required, rather than 'duly authenticated'/'duly certified' documents); art. 36 (grounds for refusing recognition or enforcement, mirroring the art. 34(2) setting-aside grounds, plus non-arbitrability and public policy, and the deference rule where an application to set aside is pending).

3. WHY THE ARBITRATION RULES ARE NOT THE PRIMARY ANSWER — AND WHEN THEY WOULD BE
UNCITRAL's FAQ draws the line expressly: 'The UNCITRAL Model Law provides a pattern that law-makers in national governments can adopt as part of their domestic legislation on arbitration. The UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules, on the other hand, are selected by parties either as part of their contract or after a dispute arises... Put simply, the Model Law is directed at States, while the Arbitration Rules are directed at potential (or actual) parties to a dispute.' (https://uncitral.un.org/en/texts/arbitration/faq, fetched 2026-11-23.) The Rules (UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules, as revised in 2010, GA Res. 65/22 (2010); with art. 1(4) as adopted 2013, GA Res. 68/109 (2013); and art. 1(5) as adopted 2021, GA Res. 76/108 (2021)) do supply tribunal composition and a competence provision (art. 21 of the Rules, which is the contractual analogue of Model Law art. 16) and an award regime (arts. 32-34 of the Rules), but they do not and cannot supply the court-intervention or recognition-and-enforcement architecture, which is state law. They are therefore a companion retrieval, not the answer.
The request is ambiguous as between a legislative template and contract-clause wording ('model arbitration text' for a 'cros-border contracts team'). Because the four listed topics are precisely the Model Law's chapter coverage and include two (court intervention; recognition and enforcement) that no contract document can create, the Model Law is the correct primary answer. If the team's real deliverable is the arbitration clause itself, the correct second retrieval is the UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (as revised in 2010) together with its model arbitration clause, plus, if the arbitration is to be administered, the chosen institution's model clause. Flag this to the instructing attorney before drafting; it changes the deliverable, not the answer to the question asked.

4. JURISDICTION: WHAT THE MODEL LAW IS AND IS NOT
No jurisdiction is identified in the request. That matters, and the following must be said plainly: the Model Law is a legislative template and has the force of law in no State by itself. It bites only through an enacting instrument in the relevant State, and then in the enacted form, which may be the 1985 text, the 2006 text, or a text with local variations. UNCITRAL notes that 'as of 2006, the standard version of the Model Law is the amended version' while 'the original 1985 text is also reproduced in view of the many national enactments based on this original version' (official page cited above).
Illustrative enacting / non-enacting States (each must be verified against the current consolidated text by the reviewing attorney before reliance, since I cannot check the consolidated statutes here):
- Singapore: Internarional Arbitration Act 1994 (2020 Rev. Ed.), Cap. 143 A — the Model Law has the force of law, subject to the modifications in the Schedule (verify s. 5 and the Schedule).
- Hong Kong SAR: Arbitration Ordinance (Cap. 609) — the Model Law text has effect with the modifications in Schedule 1 (verify s. 4 and Sch. 1).
- Germany: Zivilprozessordnung, Book 10 (ss. 1025-1066) — modelled on the Model Law.
- England and Wales: Arbitration Act 1996 — NOT a Model Law enactment. Enforcement of New York Convention awards runs through ss. 100-104 and enforcement of awards generally through s. 66 of that Act; Chapter VIII of the Model Law has no application there.
- France: Code de procédure civile, arts. 1442-1527 (as revised by Décr. no. 2011-48 of 13 Jan. 2011), with internarional enforcement at arts. 1514-1527 — not Model Law based.
- United States (federal): Federal Arbitration Act, 9 U.S.C. §§ 1-16, with the New York Convention at §§ 201-208 — not a Model Law enactment; a number of states have enacted Model Law variants for internarional arbitration, so the state of the seat/enforcement must be checked separately.
The practical instruction to the team: name the seat and every likely enforcement State, then check for each (i) whether it is an enacting State, (ii) which version it enacted (1985 or 2006), and (iii) the local variations, in particular the art. 7 option chosen and the art. 16(3) recourse model. The Model Law retrieval is the template against which those enactments are read; it is not a substitute for them.

5. DRAFTING-SIGNIFICANCE POINTS THE REVIEWER SHOULD KNOW WHEN USING THE TEXT
(a) Art. 7 has two alternatives. Option I modernises the form requirement (an agreement in writing, with writing defined functionally to cover electronic and recorded communications); Option II reproduces the 1985 writing requirement (signed document or exchange of letters, telex, telegrams or other means of telecommunication providing a record). There is therefore no single 'the' art. 7 — the enacting State's choice governs, and a clause valid under Option I may fail under an Option II enactment. Confirm the enacted option in the seat State before relying on electronic acceptance or unsigned terms.
(b) Art. 16(3) recourse models diverge. Some enactments give the court the last word on a preliminary jurisdictional ruling with no appeal; others permit immediate curial review or leave it to the setting-aside stage. Confirm which model the seat adopted before deciding whether to seek a preliminary ruling or reserve jurisdiction.
(c) Art. 5 is the pivot for court intervention and is not self-executing: it confines intervention to what the Model Law provides, but the content of those provisions (and the identity of the competent court under art. 6) is supplied by the enacting State. Anti-suit relief and court-ordered interrim measures are the areas of most divergence in practice; consult the UNCITRAL 2012 Digest of Case Law on the Model Law and CLOUT abstracts (both listed on the official page) rather than assuming uniformity.
(d) Arts. 35-36 versus the New York Convention. Chapter VIII governs recognition and enforcement inside an enacting State; enforcement in a State that is not an enacting State, or of an award rendered elsewhere, depends on the Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, New York, 10 June 1958, 330 UNTS 3, No. 4739 (entered into force 7 June 1959) — arts. III-VI — or on local law. The two regimes are close but not identical in wording (e.g. the Convention's 'binding' and 'not yet binding' formulations in art. V(1)(e) against the Model Law's art. 36(1)(a)(v)), and the Convention's art. I(3) reciprocity and commercial reservations have no counterpart in the Model Law. Do not treat art. 36 as a statement of the Convention's grounds.
(e) The Model Law contains no arbitration clause. The contract wording comes from the Rules' model clause or an institution's model clause; the Model Law supplies the legal environment in which that clause will be tested.

6. WHERE AUTHORITY IS THIN OR CONFLICTING (stated as required)
- Version conflict: the 1985 and 2006 texts coexist in force across enacting States; there is no single worldwide 'current' text. The 2006 text is the standard for new enactments but not for existing ones.
- Art. 7 internal conflict: the two options are mutually exclusive alternatives in the same article; any statement that 'the Model Law requires writing in the form of X' is incomplete without the option.
- Art. 17 regime: Chapter IV A replaced art. 17 in 2006; pre-2006 enactments still carry the older, narrower art. 17. Court-ordered interrim relief under arts. 17 H-17 I exists only in 2006-based enactments.
- Enforcement: art. 35(1) presupposes the forum State's procedural machinery and does not itself create a cause of action or a court; and the relationship between art. 36 and Convention art. V is not settled uniformly in national case law.
- Secondary sources are not primary: the Secretariat Explanatory Note, the 2012 Digest and CLOUT abstracts are aids to interpretation. Cite the enacted statute of the relevant State, and the Model Law article, as the authority.

7. RETRIEVAL CHECKLIST (what to actually pull)
1. Model Law, 1985, with amendments as adopted in 2006 — official UNCITRAL PDF (07-86998_ebook.pdf) and the official page; record the version marker 'as amended in 2006' on the file.
2. Secretariat Explanatory Note to the Model Law (2006), from the same page — for the art-by-art commentary, used as secondary only.
3. UNCITRAL 2012 Digest of Case Law on the Model Law, and CLOUT abstracts — for the divergent points in §5.
4. Status page for enacting States and the version each adopted — the decisive step for any named seat.
5. Companion: UNCITRAL Arbitration Rules (as revised in 2010, with art. 1(4) 2013 and art. 1(5) 2021) and its model clause — only if the deliverable is the clause itself.
6. Convention on the Recognition and Enforcement of Foreign Arbitral Awards, New York, 10 June 1958, 330 UNTS 3, No. 4739 — for every enforcement State that is not an enacting State.

8. BOTOM LINE FOR THE INSTRUCTING ATTORNEY
Retrieve the UNCITRAL Model Law on Internarional Commercial Arbitration (1985, as amended in 2006) as the model text for all four topics. It is the only UNCITRAL instrument that covers court intervention and recognition/enforcement at all, and UNCITRAL's own description maps it to the four topics. Then, before any clause is settled: (i) confirm whether the team needs legislative-template language or clause language; (ii) name the seat and enforcement States and verify their enactments and versions; (iii) confirm the art. 7 option and the art. 16(3) model in the seat State. This draft is for review by a qualified attorney and is not legal advice.
