JURISDICTION: United States (federal). The analysis addresses only courts to which the Federal Rules of Evidence apply by their own terms, Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a), and only the rules as originally enacted and effective July 1, 1975. State evidence law is outside the scope of this memorandum.

────────────────────────────────────────
I. QUESTIONS PRESENTED
────────────────────────────────────────
Q1. (Framing constraint) What are the original applicability provisions of the Federal Rules of Evidence, and is the answer to be given under them rather than under the current rules?
Q2. Under those original provisions, do the rules govern further procedure in an action, case, or proceeding already pending when the rules took effect?
Q3. To the extent that applying the rules in such a pending matter would not be feasible or would work injustice, what governs instead?

────────────────────────────────────────
II. SHORT ANSWERS
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. The original applicability provisions are § 1 of the Act of January 2, 1975 — Pub. L. 93-595, § 1, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926 — carried in the United States Code as the note “Effective Date and Application of Rules” to Fed. R. Evid. 1101. They are statutory, not a rule of evidence. Rule 1101 itself contains no provision addressed to actions pending when the rules took effect — neither in its original form nor in the current official print. Any answer that starts from Rule 1101 alone is looking in the wrong place.

A2. Yes. The statute provides that the rules apply to actions brought after the effective date and “also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending.” Application to further procedure is the default rule; non-application is the exception, and the party seeking it carries the work.

A3. “except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply.” The exception is measured “to the extent” — rule by rule and issue by issue — and its consequence is substitution, not nullification: the evidence law that governed in that court immediately before July 1, 1975 governs that slice of the further procedure.

────────────────────────────────────────
III. GOVERNING AUTHORITY (PRIMARY SOURCES)
────────────────────────────────────────
A. The original applicability provision — full text.

Pub. L. 93-595, § 1, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926 (note “Effective Date and Application of Rules” to Fed. R. Evid. 1101), provides:

  “That the following rules shall take effect on the one hundred and eightieth day [July 1, 1975] beginning after the date of the enactment of this Act [Jan. 2, 1975]. These rules apply to actions, cases, and proceedings brought after the rules take effect. These rules also apply to further procedure in actions, cases, and proceedings then pending, except to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice, in which event former evidentiary principles apply.”

Three drafting notes, each of which matters:
 (i) “the following rules” refers to the rules set out in § 1 of the Act itself; Congress enacted the Evidence Rules rather than allowing the Supreme Court's November 20, 1972 promulgation to take effect, so the transition rule is a statute and cannot be displaced by the Court.
 (ii) The bracketed “[July 1, 1975]” is the codifier's annotation, not statutory text. The one hundred and eightieth day beginning after January 2, 1975 is July 1, 1975.
 (iii) The provision is a rule of temporal reach only. It does not decide which courts and proceedings the rules govern (that is Rule 1101), and it does not decide which evidence is admissible (that is the remainder of the rules).

B. The surviving statutory formula — 28 U.S.C. § 2074, as reproduced in the statutory appendix to the Federal Rules of Evidence:

  “… shall take effect no earlier than December 1 of the year in which such rule is so transmitted unless otherwise provided by law. The Supreme Court may fix the extent such rule shall apply to proceedings then pending, except that the Supreme Court shall not require the application of such rule to further proceedings then pending to the extent that, in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending, the application of such rule in such proceedings would not be feasible or would work injustice, in which event the former rule applies.
  (b) Any such rule creating, abolishing, or modifying an evidentiary privilege shall have no force or effect unless approved by Act of Congress.”
  (Added Pub. L. 100-702, tit. IV, § 401(a), Nov. 19, 1988, 102 Stat. 4649, eff. Dec. 1, 1988.)

Why it matters: (1) Congress re-enacted the identical “not feasible or would work injustice” formula in 1988, which shows the formula is a durable feature of federal evidence rulemaking rather than a 1975 artifact; (2) the 1988 text expressly assigns the judgment to “the court in which such proceedings are pending,” which the 1975 text does not — a real textual difference, discussed at IV.5; (3) § 2074 governs amendments taking effect after December 1, 1988 and does NOT govern the 1975 transition, which is governed by § 1 of Pub. L. 93-595.

C. Rule 1101 — the other applicability provision (current official text, Fed. R. Evid. 1101(a)-(d)):

  “(a) TO COURTS AND JUDGES. These rules apply to proceedings before: United States district courts; United States bankruptcy and magistrate judges; United States courts of appeals; the United States Court of Federal Claims; and the district courts of Guam, the Virgin Islands, and the Northern Mariana Islands.
  (b) TO CASES AND PROCEEDINGS. These rules apply in: civil cases and proceedings, including bankruptcy, admiralty, and maritime cases; criminal cases and proceedings; and contempt proceedings, except those in which the court may act summarily.
  (c) RULES ON PRIVILEGE. The rules on privilege apply to all stages of a case or proceeding.
  (d) EXCEPTIONS. These rules — except for those on privilege — do not apply to the following: (1) the court's determination, under Rule 104(a), on a preliminary question of fact governing admissibility; (2) grand-jury proceedings; and (3) miscellaneous proceedings such as: extradition or rendition; issuing an arrest warrant, criminal summons, or search warrant; a preliminary examination in a criminal case; sentencing; …”

Point: Rule 1101 answers “which courts and which kinds of proceedings.” It does not answer “which stage of a case already under way.” The two questions are cumulative: a proceeding must be within Rule 1101, and the particular further procedure must not fall within § 1's exception.

D. Background law supplying content to “former evidentiary principles”: Funk v. United States, 290 U.S. 371 (1933); Wolfle v. United States, 291 U.S. 7 (1934) (federal courts' evidence law as general federal law, not the law of the forum State); Erie R.R. Co. v. Tompkins, 304 U.S. 64 (1938), together with former 28 U.S.C. § 1652 (state law as the rule of decision in diversity). Consequence: what “former evidentiary principles” were depends on the court and the issue — in diversity cases, frequently state law; in federal-question and criminal cases, the federal common law and federal statutes as they stood before July 1, 1975.

E. Parallel provisions, cited for structural comparison only (same formula; § 1's language tracks them): Fed. R. Civ. P. 86(a); Fed. R. Crim. P. 59. Text to be verified against the current official print before filing (see § VII).

────────────────────────────────────────
IV. ANALYSIS
────────────────────────────────────────
1. The default is application. The third sentence of § 1 is permissive in form and mandatory in effect: the rules “also apply to further procedure.” There is no threshold finding a court must make before applying them to a pending case, and no requirement that a party opt in. The exception is drafted as a limit on application (“except to the extent that …”), which places the burden on the party seeking to avoid a rule.

2. What “further procedure” reaches. “Then pending” fixes the reference date at July 1, 1975. “Further procedure” is procedural action taken after that date. It reaches, at minimum: evidentiary objections and rulings; offers of proof; examination of witnesses; trial and retrial; post-trial motions in which evidence is received; further proceedings on remand; and appellate steps in which evidence rulings are made or reviewed. It does not reach matters already concluded before the effective date: evidence already admitted, rulings already made, and trials already completed. The provision addresses further procedure; it does not reopen a record or create a ground to relitigate a final pre-July 1, 1975 ruling. A retrial or remand occurring after July 1, 1975 in a case commenced earlier is “further procedure in a[n] action … then pending” and is governed by the rules, subject to the exception. (That last sentence is a textual inference; no decision construing the point was located — see § V.)

3. The exception: two independent triggers, measured “to the extent.”
 • “not feasible” — practical or administrative impossibility, or gross disproportion: evidence already taken under former procedures; a trial in mid-course when the rules took effect; discovery conducted under different privilege assumptions; inability to reconstruct a record to satisfy a new requirement.
 • “would work injustice” — unfair prejudice, reliance, surprise: a party shaped its case on the former principle; a protection available under former law would be lost; retroactive application would deprive a party of a fair opportunity to present or contest evidence.
 • “to the extent” — the relief is severable. It operates rule by rule and issue by issue. WhOLESALE refusal is available only if the infeasibility or injustice is itself wholesale; the ordinary case is a targeted carve-out with the balance of the rules in force.
 • Burden and record. The statute prescribes no procedure. Practically, the party seeking the exception must identify (a) the specific rule, (b) the specific further procedure, (c) the former principle, and (d) the concrete infeasibility or injustice, and must do so on the record through an objection or motion in limine with a proffer. Preservation is governed by Fed. R. Evid. 103.
 • Interaction with Rule 1101(c). The privilege rules apply “to all stages of a case or proceeding.” That cuts against a carve-out for an Article V privilege rule and requires a correspondingly stronger showing of reliance or injustice.

4. What “former evidentiary principles” means. It means the evidence law that would have governed in that court immediately before July 1, 1975: federal common-law evidence doctrine, applicable federal statutes, and — in diversity — state law under Erie and former 28 U.S.C. § 1652. It does not mean “no rules”: the exception substitutes a body of law; it does not create a vacuum. Because that law varied by circuit and by issue, a movant must state the former principle with specificity and cite pre-1975 authority for it.

5. Who decides, and review. The 1975 text is impersonal: it does not say who judges feasibility or injustice. The 1988 codification, 28 U.S.C. § 2074, supplies the answer for later rules — “in the opinion of the court in which such proceedings are pending.” That is strong evidence that the determination belongs to the trial court and is discretionary. Inference, flagged as such and not a holding: the court in which the further procedure is pending decides; appellate review is for abuse of discretion; the ruling is fact-specific and reviewable only on a developed record.

6. Civil, criminal, or other proceedings — the original provision does not distinguish. Section 1 uses a single composite phrase, “actions, cases, and proceedings,” and states one default and one exception for all of them. The answer therefore does not change if the pending matter is civil or criminal. What does vary is Rule 1101's categorical reach (grand jury, preliminary examination in a criminal case, sentencing, extradition, warrant proceedings, and the other Rule 1101(d) exclusions), which is a separate filter applied first: a proceeding excluded by Rule 1101(d) never reaches § 1 at all. The harness's second research question (civil vs. criminal) is thus answered by the text: no differentiation.

7. Actions commenced on or after July 1, 1975. The exception is unavailable. It is keyed to an action “then pending,” not to when the underlying events occurred. A case filed in August 1975 receives the rules even as to pre-1975 conduct, subject to other and distinct constraints: the substantive-right limitation in § 2 of the Act (verify text, § VII), constitutional limits on retroactivity, and ordinary Erie analysis. Corollary: § 1 is not a general retroactivity doctrine and should not be cited as one.

8. Current status. The 1975 transition is spent. Section 1 has no continuing operation except as to matters still pending in 1975 and their further procedure. For amendments taking effect after December 1, 1988, the analogous protection is 28 U.S.C. § 2074, and the modern practitioner confronting a newly amended evidence rule should look to § 2074 and to the rule's own effective-date note, not to § 1.

V. WHERE THE AUTHORITY IS THIN OR CONFLICTING
────────────────────────────────────────
• No Supreme Court or court of appeals decision construing the savings clause of § 1 was located. If the clause was litigated at all, it was in the late 1970s; it is not a live issue.
• The strongest interpretive guidance is (i) the identical formula in Fed. R. Civ. P. 86(a) (1938) and its criminal-rules counterpart, and (ii) the 1988 re-enactment in 28 U.S.C. § 2074. Both are persuasive, neither is controlling on the meaning of the 1975 text.
• Genuinely open points: (a) decision-maker — silent in 1975, supplied in 1988; (b) timing of the “injustice” assessment — at the ruling, or in hindsight on appeal; (c) whether a court may decline the rules wholesale rather than rule by rule; (d) how the exception interacts with Rule 1101(c)'s “all stages” command for privileges.
• A potential doctrinal confusion to avoid: the substantive-right limitation in § 2 of the Act and the “work injustice” exception in § 1 can overlap factually but are distinct — § 2 constrains the validity of the rules; § 1 allocates which body of evidence law governs a slice of further procedure. Do not argue one as if it were the other. (Verify § 2 text before relying — § VII.)

VI. PRACTICE TOOLKIT
────────────────────────────────────────
A. Checklist for a matter arguably within § 1.
 1. Fix the commencement date and document that the action was pending on July 1, 1975.
 2. Identify each precise further procedure at issue (each step after July 1, 1975), not “the trial” generally.
 3. Identify the specific rule whose application is contested — not “the rules.”
 4. State the former principle with citation to pre-1975 authority, and state why it applied in this court (federal common law, statute, or state law under Erie).
 5. Show reliance concretely: what was done, when, and on what assumption.
 6. Show that the resulting prejudice cannot now be cured.
 7. Limit the request: rule by rule, issue by issue; expressly disclaim any wholesale displacement.
 8. Preserve: contemporaneous objection or motion in limine, offer of proof, Fed. R. Evid. 103.
 9. Anticipate the counter-arguments: application is the statutory default, and Rule 1101(c) puts privilege at “all stages.”
 10. If the ruling is adverse, frame the appeal as abuse of discretion on the developed factual record.

B. Model paragraph (adapt before use).
 “This action was commenced on [date], before July 1, 1975, and was therefore pending when the Federal Rules of Evidence took effect. Pub. L. 93-595, § 1, Jan. 2, 1975, 88 Stat. 1926. [Movant] does not seek to displace the rules generally; they ‘also apply to further procedure’ in this action. Id. [Movant] asks the Court to decline to apply Rule [___] to [identify the further procedure] only ‘to the extent that application of the rules would not be feasible, or would work injustice.’ Id. Application of Rule [___] here would work injustice: [party] conducted [the discovery / the examination / the prior trial] in reliance on [former principle], which then governed in this circuit, and [describe the concrete prejudice — evidence lost, witness unavailable, defect incapable of cure]. Under § 1, ‘former evidentiary principles apply’ to that extent — namely, [state the former principle]. The relief requested is limited to [scope] and leaves the balance of the rules in force for all further procedure.”

C. Short form for an objection at trial.
 “Objection — Rule [___] does not govern this further procedure. This action was pending on July 1, 1975, and application here would work injustice for the reasons stated on the record. Pub. L. 93-595, § 1, 88 Stat. 1926. Former evidentiary principles apply, namely [principle].”

This is a research draft for attorney review, not legal advice.
